q: Your car has broken down on a busy main road and you have a warning triangle. How far behind your car should you put it?
options: At least 25 metres
At least 45 metres
At least 15 metres
At least 100 metres
explain: You should put a warning triangle on the road at least 45 metres (147 feet) behind your broken-down vehicle, on the same side of the road. Take great care when placing or retrieving it.

q: You've broken down on the hard shoulder of a motorway. You have a warning triangle in your boot. What should you do with it?
options: Place it 45 metres behind your car
Place it 100 metres behind your car
Don't use it on the motorway
Place it on the roof of your car
explain: You should never use a warning triangle on a motorway, and DO NOT place one on the carriageway. Instead, get well away from your vehicle and moving traffic and call for help.

q: Your car has broken down on a narrow road and is partly blocking the carriageway. How should you warn other traffic?
options: Switch on your hazard warning lights
Leave your headlights on main beam
Sound your horn at approaching vehicles
Stand in the road and wave traffic past
explain: If your broken-down vehicle is causing an obstruction, warn other traffic by using your hazard warning lights. Don't stand, or let anyone else stand, between your vehicle and oncoming traffic.

q: You've broken down on a country road at night and need to get out of your car. What should you wear to help other road users see you?
options: Reflective clothing
Dark, warm clothing
Clothing the same colour as your car
Anything, if your hazard lights are on
explain: Help other road users see you by wearing light-coloured or fluorescent clothing in daylight and reflective clothing at night or in poor visibility.

q: Your car has broken down on a main road at night and you're waiting for help. Why shouldn't you stand at the back of your car?
options: You might stop other drivers seeing your lights
Your exhaust fumes could make you dizzy
Recovery drivers will find the car harder to spot
Your hazard lights could dazzle you
explain: Don't stand, or let anybody else stand, between your vehicle and oncoming traffic. At night or in poor visibility, don't stand where you'll prevent other road users seeing your lights.

q: You're driving on a motorway when a warning light comes on and you need to stop. Where is the safest place to stop?
options: On the hard shoulder
In an emergency area
At a service area
On the verge of a slip road
explain: On motorways and other high-speed roads, the safest place to stop is a service area. Emergency areas and hard shoulders are places of relative safety, but hard shoulders give less protection because they're so close to high-speed traffic.

q: You've stopped in a lay-by on a busy dual carriageway after a breakdown. Why should you and your passengers keep well away from your car and the moving traffic?
options: Your car could be hit and pushed into you
So recovery drivers can see the car clearly
So the engine can cool down more safely
So you don't breathe in exhaust fumes
explain: You and your passengers should, where possible, keep well away from your vehicle and moving traffic. Otherwise moving traffic could collide with your vehicle, forcing it into you.

q: You stop to help at the scene of a collision on a busy road. How should you warn other traffic?
options: Leave your headlights on main beam
Sound your horn repeatedly
Switch on your hazard warning lights
Park across the road to block it
explain: If you're involved in a collision or stop to give assistance, use your hazard warning lights to warn other traffic, and put on high-visibility clothing if you have it.

q: You arrive at a crash scene where several cars are damaged. Why should you ask the drivers to switch off their engines?
options: To save fuel while they wait
To reduce the risk of fire
To stop the batteries going flat
So the police can check the engines
explain: Further collisions and fire are the main dangers following a crash. You should ask drivers to switch off their engines and ask everyone to stop smoking.

q: You're at the scene of a collision where people are injured. You call the emergency services. What should you tell them?
options: Only the registration numbers of the vehicles
Only your own name and address
Which driver you think caused it
The location and details of any casualties
explain: Contact the emergency services on 999 and provide full details of the incident location and any casualties. You can use an emergency telephone, a mobile phone, or your vehicle's SOS button if it has one.

q: You're calling the emergency services from the scene of a crash on a dual carriageway. Which extra detail will help them reach it quickly?
options: The make and model of your car
The direction of traffic involved
The time you set off on your journey
The weather forecast for the area
explain: The emergency services need the exact location of the incident, including the direction of traffic (for example, northbound), and the number of vehicles involved. Also tell them about the condition of any casualties.

q: You arrive at a crash. A driver is still in their car and seems to be injured, but there's no threat of fire or further danger. What should you do?
options: Pull them out of the car straight away
Help them walk to the side of the road
Lay them down on the road surface
Leave them in the car unless in danger
explain: DO NOT move injured people from their vehicles unless they're in immediate danger. Keep them warm and reassure them until the emergency services arrive.

q: A motorcyclist has been injured in a collision and is lying in the road, still wearing their helmet. What should you do about the helmet?
options: Take it off to make them comfortable
Only remove it if it's essential
Take it off so you can check for injuries
Lift their head and loosen it
explain: DO NOT remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless it's essential and you're trained to do so. Keep the casualty warm and reassure them while you wait for the emergency services.

q: You've been involved in a collision on a busy road. Your passengers aren't hurt. What should you do with them?
options: Keep them in the car with seat belts on
Ask them to direct the traffic around you
Ask them to stand behind the car as a warning
Move them to a place of relative safety
explain: You should move uninjured people away from the vehicles to a place of relative safety, where they're less likely to be at risk from moving traffic.

q: You've been involved in a collision in which someone was hurt. You've called 999. What should you do next?
options: Stay until the emergency services arrive
Drive home and phone the police later
Leave once another driver stops to help
Leave a note on the other car and go
explain: You should stay at the scene until the emergency services arrive. Be prepared to give first aid and to exchange details.

q: An injured person at a crash scene asks you for a drink of water. What should you do?
options: Give them small sips of water
Give them a hot, sweet drink
Don't give them anything to drink
Give them a drink if they seem thirsty
explain: DO NOT give casualties anything to eat or drink. Keep them warm, dry and as comfortable as you can, and reassure them until help arrives.

q: You're looking after a casualty at a crash scene while waiting for an ambulance. They're conscious but upset. How can you help them?
options: Encourage them to walk about to stay alert
Leave them alone so they can rest
Keep them warm and reassure them
Ask them who caused the crash
explain: Try to keep casualties warm, dry and as comfortable as you can. Give reassurance confidently and try not to leave them alone or let them wander into the path of other traffic.

q: You're giving first aid at the scene of a crash and remember the letters DR ABC. What does the D stand for?
options: Danger
Doctor
Distance
Dial
explain: D stands for Danger: check that it's safe to approach. The letters stand for Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing and Circulation.

q: You reach a casualty who's lying still after a collision. It's safe to approach. How should you check whether they respond?
options: Splash some cold water onto their face
Sit them up and loudly call their name
Shake their head gently from side to side
Gently shake their shoulders and ask loudly
explain: Try to get a response by gently shaking the casualty's shoulders and asking loudly 'Are you all right?' If they respond, check for injuries.

q: A casualty at a crash scene doesn't respond when you speak to them. How should you open their airway?
options: Lift their chin forward with your fingers
Tilt their head down onto their chest
Turn their head sharply to one side
Sit them upright, leaning against the car
explain: If there's no response, open the casualty's airway by placing your fingers under their chin and lifting it forward. Then check that they're breathing normally.

q: A pedestrian injured in a collision is lying on the pavement. They're unconscious but breathing normally. What should you do until medical help arrives?
options: Start chest compressions straight away
Place them in the recovery position
Sit them up against a wall
Leave them alone to look for help
explain: If the casualty is unconscious and breathing, place them in the recovery position until medical help arrives. Only start CPR if there are no signs of breathing.

q: An adult casualty isn't breathing and you start CPR. How far should you press down on the centre of their chest?
options: About 1 to 2 centimetres
About 3 to 4 centimetres
About 5 to 6 centimetres
About 10 to 12 centimetres
explain: Interlock your fingers, place them in the centre of the casualty's chest and press down hard and fast, around 5 to 6 centimetres.

q: You're giving CPR to an adult at the scene of a crash. How fast should you press on their chest?
options: About twice a second
About once a second
About once every two seconds
About five times a second
explain: When giving CPR to an adult, press down hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second.

q: A baby involved in a crash isn't breathing. How should you give chest compressions?
options: Both hands, 5 to 6 centimetres deep
One hand, pressing as hard as possible
Heel of one hand, on the stomach
Two fingers, a third of the chest depth
explain: For infants, use two fingers in the middle of the chest and press down about a third of the chest depth. For a child you may only need one hand, and shouldn't press down as far as for an adult.

q: You've started CPR on a casualty who wasn't breathing. When should you stop?
options: After about two minutes of compressions
When they breathe or a medic takes over
As soon as you've done 30 compressions
When a police officer arrives at the scene
explain: Don't stop CPR until the casualty starts breathing again or a medical professional takes over.

q: A casualty at a crash scene is bleeding heavily from a leg wound. There's nothing in the wound. What should you do?
options: Wash the wound with clean water first
Leave it uncovered to let it clot
Apply firm pressure over the wound
Keep the leg moving so it doesn't stiffen
explain: If nothing is embedded, apply firm pressure over the wound to stem the flow of blood. As soon as practical, fasten a pad to the wound with a bandage or length of cloth, using the cleanest material available.

q: A casualty has a piece of glass stuck in a bleeding wound on their arm. What should you do?
options: Pull the glass out, then press on the wound
Press firmly on the glass to stop the bleeding
Leave it in and build up padding either side
Wash the glass out with water
explain: Don't remove anything that's stuck in a wound. Taking care not to press on the object, build up padding on either side of it.

q: A driver has been burned in a vehicle fire. The flames are out. How long should you cool the burn with clean, cool water?
options: For about 1 minute
For at least 5 minutes
For no more than 10 minutes
For at least 20 minutes
explain: Cool the burn for at least 20 minutes with plenty of clean, cool water. Cover the burn with cling film if available.

q: You're helping someone who has a burn on their arm. Some of their clothing is stuck to it. What should you do?
options: Pull the clothing off gently
Peel it away after cooling the burn
Leave it there and cool the burn
Soak it, then pull it off quickly
explain: Don't try to remove anything that's sticking to a burn. Cool the burn with plenty of clean, cool water and cover it with cling film if available.

q: You've stopped to help at a crash. What are the main dangers at the scene?
options: Theft from the vehicles
Further collisions and fire
Traffic jams and delays
Flat batteries in the cars
explain: Further collisions and fire are the main dangers following a crash. Approach any vehicle involved with care, watching out for spilt oil or broken glass, switch off all engines and warn other traffic if possible.

q: You've stopped to help at a crash. Why should you take care as you approach the damaged vehicles?
options: There may be spilt oil or broken glass
You could disturb evidence for the police
The drivers may not want your help
You might be blamed for the damage
explain: Further collisions and fire are the main dangers following a crash. Approach any vehicle involved with care, watching out for spilt oil or broken glass.

q: You arrive at a collision involving a tanker carrying dangerous goods. People appear to be trapped in a car beside it. What should you do?
options: Try to rescue them as quickly as you can
Move closer so that you can reassure them
Ask a passer-by to help you pull them free
Keep well away and call the emergency services
explain: If an incident involves a vehicle carrying dangerous goods, keep well away and don't be tempted to try to rescue casualties, as you could become one yourself. Switch off engines, DO NOT smoke, and call the emergency services.

q: A lorry carrying a flammable load has been involved in a crash. You need to call the emergency services. What should you do?
options: Use your mobile phone right beside the lorry
Give details of its labels from a safe distance
Wait until the fire service has arrived
Only report the number of people hurt
explain: Call the emergency services and give as much information as possible about the labels and markings on the vehicle. DO NOT use a mobile phone close to a vehicle carrying flammable loads.

q: You see this symbol on a hazard warning plate. Which kind of vehicle displays plates like this?
options: A vehicle carrying livestock
A tanker carrying dangerous goods
A vehicle with an overhanging load
A lorry weighing over 7.5 tonnes
explain: Road tankers and vehicles carrying tank containers of dangerous goods display hazard warning plates; this symbol shows a toxic substance. If such a vehicle is involved in an incident, keep well away and give the emergency services details of its markings.

q: You've hit a parked car while manoeuvring, causing damage. The owner comes out to speak to you. What MUST you give them?
options: Only your mobile phone number and email
Only the name of your insurance company
Your driving licence for them to keep
Your name, address and vehicle registration
explain: If you're involved in a collision that causes damage or injury, you MUST stop and give your own and the vehicle owner's name and address, and the vehicle's registration number, to anyone with reasonable grounds for requiring them.

q: You've damaged a parked car and can't find the owner to give them your details. What MUST you do?
options: Report it to the police within 24 hours
Report it to the police within 7 days
Report it to your insurer within a month
Nothing, if the damage is minor
explain: If you don't give your name and address at the time of the collision, you MUST report it to the police as soon as reasonably practicable, and in any case within 24 hours.

q: You're involved in a crash in which someone is injured, and you can't produce your insurance certificate at the time. Within what time MUST you produce it for the police?
options: 24 hours
48 hours
7 days
14 days
explain: If another person is injured and you don't produce your insurance certificate at the time, you MUST report the crash to the police as soon as possible and within 24 hours, and produce your certificate for the police within seven days.

q: You've had a minor collision and exchanged details with the other driver. You don't intend to make a claim. Should you tell your insurance company?
options: Yes, even though you're not claiming
No, only if you decide to claim
No, only if the police were involved
Only if the other driver asks you to
explain: You must report an accident to your insurance company, even if you're not planning to make a claim.

q: Your car breaks down on a level crossing. What should you do first?
options: Try to restart the engine several times
Get everyone out and clear of the crossing
Phone your breakdown recovery service
Stay in the car with your hazard lights on
explain: If your vehicle breaks down on a level crossing, get everyone out of the vehicle and clear of the crossing immediately. Then use a railway telephone, if available, to tell the signal operator.

q: You've broken down on a level crossing and everyone is safely clear. There's a railway telephone nearby. What should you do?
options: Call a breakdown service on your mobile
Wait for the barriers to come down
Walk along the line to warn the driver
Use it to tell the signal operator
explain: Use the railway telephone to tell the signal operator, and follow the instructions you're given. Only move the vehicle clear of the crossing if there's time before a train arrives.

q: Your car has stalled on a level crossing and you're trying to push it clear. The alarm sounds and the amber light comes on. What should you do?
options: Leave the car and get clear immediately
Keep pushing, as there's still time
Get back in and try to restart it
Stand by the car and wave to warn the train
explain: Only try to move the vehicle clear if there's time before a train arrives. If the alarm sounds or the amber light comes on, leave the vehicle and get clear of the crossing immediately.

q: You're driving when you see flames coming from under your car's bonnet. You stop safely. What should you do?
options: Open the bonnet to put the fire out
Pour water into the engine compartment
Get everyone out and call the fire brigade
Drive on quickly to the nearest garage
explain: If your vehicle catches fire, get the occupants out quickly and to a safe place, then call the fire brigade. Don't try to put out a fire in the engine compartment, as opening the bonnet will make the fire flare.

q: You're driving through a tunnel when the traffic ahead comes to a stop. What's the minimum gap you should leave between you and the vehicle in front?
options: At least 1 metre
At least 2 metres
At least 3 metres
At least 5 metres
explain: If you have to stop in a tunnel, leave at least a 5-metre gap between you and the vehicle in front. When moving, allow at least a two-second gap in tunnels where visibility is reduced.

q: You're deaf and are planning a long car journey. What does The Highway Code recommend you do before you set off?
options: Register for the 999 text service
Fit a flashing amber beacon to your car
Plan a route that avoids all motorways
Display a sign saying you're deaf
explain: If you're deaf, hard of hearing or speech impaired, it's recommended that you register for the 999 text service (emergencySMS.net) before making a journey.

q: You're approaching an incident on a dual carriageway. A traffic officer is directing traffic past the scene. What MUST you do?
options: Follow the traffic officer's directions
Pass on whichever side looks clearest
Stop and wait for the police to arrive
Only follow directions from the police
explain: The emergency services, traffic officers and recovery workers may need to work in the carriageway at an incident. You MUST follow any directions given by police or traffic officers as to whether you can safely pass the incident or obstruction.

q: Part of your load falls from your trailer onto a quiet road in a village. What should you do?
options: Leave it there; the council will clear it
Phone 999 and wait in your car
Remove it, but only if it's safe to do so
Drive on and report it next week
explain: On roads other than motorways and high-speed roads, you should only remove an obstruction if it's safe to do so. On a motorway or other high-speed road, DO NOT remove it yourself; stop in a place of relative safety and call 999.

q: You're driving on a dual carriageway and see emergency vehicles with flashing lights a long way ahead. What should you do?
options: Speed up to get past before it's blocked
Slow down and be ready to change lane or stop
Keep your speed and watch the incident closely
Flash your headlights to warn the drivers ahead
explain: If you see emergency or incident support vehicles with flashing lights in the distance, there may be an incident ahead. Slow down and be prepared to move safely into another lane or stop. You MUST follow any directions from police or traffic officers.

q: You're driving on a dual carriageway. There's been a crash on the other side of the central reservation and the emergency services are already there. What should you do?
options: Slow down so you can get a better look
Stop on the verge to see if you can help
Use your phone to film the scene as you pass
Keep going and concentrate on the road ahead
explain: When passing the scene of an incident, remain alert for hazards but don't slow down unnecessarily, for example if it's on the other side of a dual carriageway. Focus on the road ahead, as a lack of attention could cause another collision or congestion.

q: You have a disability that prevents you from getting out of your car. Your car breaks down on a motorway. What should you do?
options: Switch on hazard lights, stay in and call 999
Try to get out and wait on the hard shoulder
Flash your headlights at passing drivers
Open the door and wave to passing drivers
explain: If a disability prevents you following the usual breakdown advice, switch on your hazard warning lights, stay in your vehicle with your seat belt on, and call 999 immediately and ask for the police. Alternatively, press your SOS button if your vehicle has one.

q: You're filling up at a petrol station and accidentally spill some diesel on the forecourt. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as it'll evaporate quickly
Report it to the attendant straight away
Wipe it with a cloth and drive off
Drive off before it spreads further
explain: Any spilled fuel should be reported to the petrol station attendant immediately. Diesel spillage is dangerous to other road users, particularly motorcyclists, as it greatly reduces the grip between tyres and the road surface.
